questions.question: Bronze is a hard metal made of about 88 parts copper to 12 parts tin, melted together and cooled into one evenly mixed solid. Chemists count it as a solution. Which part is the solvent, and why?
questions.answer: Copper, as there is more of it
choices: Copper, as there is more of it
Tin, as there is less of it
Tin, as it makes the copper harder
Tin, as it is spread all through the copper
questions.context: The solvent is the part a solution holds the most of, and the solute is the part spread through it, so in bronze the copper is the solvent and the tin a solute dissolved in it. Tin does make bronze harder than pure copper, but that does not decide which part is the solvent. A solution need not be a liquid: brass and sterling silver are solid solutions too, and chemists call such solutions alloys.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade names the solute and solvent of a solution by which part there is more of, and shows that solutions can be solids.

questions.question: Rain, rivers, the sea and the watery part of blood all carry substances dissolved in water, and chemists call water the universal solvent. What does the name mean?
questions.answer: It dissolves more substances than any other liquid
choices: It dissolves more substances than any other liquid
It dissolves the very substances other liquids cannot
It is the solvent in every solution in the world
It dissolves things faster than any other liquid
questions.context: Water dissolves more substances than any other liquid, which is why it carries dissolved minerals and nutrients wherever it goes, through the air, the ground and the body. Still, it cannot dissolve everything, and other liquids are solvents too: iodine dissolves so poorly in water that the antiseptic tincture of iodine, put on cuts, is made with alcohol.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade calls water the universal solvent because it dissolves more substances than any other liquid.

questions.question: When the tide goes out, a rock pool is left cut off from the sea, full of ordinary seawater. All through a hot, sunny afternoon, much of the water in the pool evaporates. What happens to the concentration of salt in the pool?
questions.answer: It rises, as the same salt is in less water
choices: It rises, as the same salt is in less water
It falls, as the salt goes off with the water
It stays the same, as no salt has been added
It falls, as less salt water is left in the pool
questions.context: Concentration is how much solute a given amount of solution holds. Evaporation takes away only water, so the salt left behind is crowded into less of it: seawater holds about 35 grams of salt in each kilogram, and a sun-baked rock pool can reach 50 or more. Rain does the opposite, diluting the pool with fresh water.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade defines concentration as the amount of solute in a given amount of solution and asks how it changes when solvent is lost or added.

questions.question: A geologist drops a walnut-sized lump of rock salt, the mineral halite, into a large beaker of water. Into a second beaker of the same water she drops the same mass of rock salt, crushed to small grains. Neither beaker is stirred. Which salt is gone first, and why?
questions.answer: The grains, as more of their surface meets the water
choices: The grains, as more of their surface meets the water
The grains, as small bits of salt are softer than a lump
Both at once, as each holds the same mass of salt
The lump, as water seeps deep into its many cracks
questions.context: Water can only work on a solid where it touches it. Crushing the lump bares far more surface to the water, so the grains dissolve much faster; the lump holds the same mass of salt, but most of it is hidden inside, away from the water.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards ask students to predict and explain how surface area changes how fast a solid dissolves.

questions.question: A student drops a blue crystal of copper sulfate into a beaker of cold water and an identical crystal into a beaker of hot water. She stirs neither one. The crystal in the hot water is gone long before the other. Why does the hotter water dissolve it faster?
questions.answer: Its particles move faster and strike the crystal more often
choices: Its particles move faster and strike the crystal more often
Its heat melts the crystal into a blue liquid first
Its heat turns the crystal into a new substance
Its particles grow bigger and push the crystal apart
questions.context: Heating water gives its particles more energy, so they move faster, strike the crystal more often and carry its particles off sooner. The crystal dissolves rather than melts, no new substance forms, and the water's particles stay the same size however hot it gets.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards ask students to explain, with particles, why a solid dissolves faster in warmer water.

questions.question: A student pours equal scoops of Epsom salt, the crystals used in soaks for sore muscles, into two beakers of warm water. She stirs one beaker and leaves the other still, and the stirred salt is gone far sooner. Why does stirring speed up the dissolving?
questions.answer: It keeps bringing fresh water to the crystals
choices: It keeps bringing fresh water to the crystals
It splits the salt's particles into smaller bits
It lets the water hold more of the salt in all
It helps the salt react with the water sooner
questions.context: The water right next to a crystal soon fills with dissolved salt and takes in more only slowly; stirring sweeps it away and brings fresh water up against the crystal. Stirring changes how fast the salt dissolves, not how much the water can hold, no particle is split, and dissolving makes no new substance, so nothing reacts.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards ask why agitation, stirring or shaking, speeds up dissolving.

questions.question: A student stirs spoonful after spoonful of potassium nitrate, a white salt, into a beaker of water at room temperature. At last some crystals stay on the bottom, because the solution is saturated. Which change will get more of those crystals to dissolve?
questions.answer: Warming the water in the beaker
choices: Warming the water in the beaker
Stirring the water much faster
Crushing the crystals to a powder
Leaving the beaker to stand for days
questions.context: A saturated solution holds all the solute it can at its temperature, and stirring, crushing or waiting only make a solid dissolve faster, never make room for more. Warmer water holds more of most solids, and potassium nitrate is a strong case: water near boiling holds more than seven times as much as water at 20 degrees Celsius.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the saturated solution and that temperature, unlike stirring or crushing, changes how much of a solid can dissolve.

questions.question: Oxygen gas is dissolved in the water of a pond. Over a long, hot summer the pond warms from 20 to 30 degrees Celsius. How does the amount of oxygen its water can hold change?
questions.answer: It falls, as warm water holds less gas
choices: It falls, as warm water holds less gas
It rises, as warm water dissolves more
It stays the same, as only solids change
It stays the same, as the air above it has not changed
questions.context: Unlike most solids, gases dissolve less in warmer water, because heat helps their particles escape it: fresh water at 20 degrees Celsius can hold about 9 milligrams of oxygen in a litre, but at 30 degrees only about 7.6. That is why hot, calm summer weather can leave pond fish short of oxygen, while cold, tumbling streams hold plenty.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade solutions units contrast solids with gases, which dissolve less in warmer water, and use the oxygen fish breathe as the example.

questions.question: A sealed bottle of fizzy water stands on a shelf, and no bubbles can be seen in it. When its cap is twisted off, bubbles stream up through the water. Why do the bubbles appear only now?
questions.answer: Less gas can stay dissolved once the pressure drops
choices: Less gas can stay dissolved once the pressure drops
The water starts to boil as the pressure drops
Air rushes in and forms bubbles all through the water
Air rushes in and reacts with the water to make a gas
questions.context: At the bottling plant, carbon dioxide is forced into chilled water under pressure and the tight cap keeps the pressure in, and the more pressure a gas is under, the more of it a liquid can hold. Opening the bottle drops the pressure to that of ordinary air, so the carbon dioxide the water can no longer keep comes out as bubbles. The bubbles are carbon dioxide, not air, and the water is far too cool to boil.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade solutions units use fizzy water to show a gas dissolved in a liquid, which comes out of solution when the pressure drops.

870af2b034.why: Judge (medium, grade) and the lead: the key, nitrogen, repeated T2 earths-four-spheres' fact that air is mostly nitrogen, so a student could answer without the solvent rule. The rule is now applied to a case no lower unit asks, bronze, a solid solution (F29): copper is the solvent as there is more of it. The judge's rubbing-alcohol case was not used, since sources disagree on whether its water or its alcohol is the solvent. Judge (medium): the weak carbon-dioxide choice is gone; the wrong choices are the reversed rule, a true but irrelevant reason (tin hardens it), and the solute's own description. Same fact (F1, F2).

dd082f2684.why: Judge (high, grade) and the lead: the key, water's slightly charged ends, is the core fact of T4 waters-sticky-properties. The question now asks what the name 'universal solvent' means, within this unit's scope, and keys the USGS sense (more substances than any other liquid, F4). The judge's wrong choices ('every substance there is', 'any amount') were not used: everyday sense (sand, a sugar heap) rules them out. The wrong choices are now three other readings that stay live: a specialist for what others cannot dissolve, the solvent of every solution, the fastest solvent. The fact-check's size remark (hydrogen against water) no longer applies, as the size choice is gone. Facts F4, F7.

adef2d55ac.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'It falls, as the Sun's heat breaks the salt down' was T1's own misconception, already taught against. It is replaced, as the judge proposed, by 'It falls, as less salt water is left in the pool', which mistakes the amount of solution for concentration. Stem, key, context and fact unchanged.

4a79b01ab3.why: Fact-check (error): one tenfold dilution cannot turn deep purple pale pink, since the two shades are about a hundredfold apart (F13, F31). The stem now says 'a much paler purple', and the tenth choice 'as the colour is so much paler'. Judge (medium): the silly 'Ten times as much' is replaced, as the judge proposed, by 'Less, as the water has broken some of it down' (dilution taken for a reaction). The question still asks the amount, not the new concentration, so no arithmetic is asked. Same key and fact.

438faa09c4.why: Fact-check (uncertain): a fist-sized lump (about 540 g) needs about 1.5 litres of water to dissolve at all, so in a beaker neither salt would ever be gone. The lump is now walnut-sized and the beaker large (F30). Judge (medium): the weak 'The lump, as its weight drags it down' is replaced, as the judge proposed, by a second 'grains' choice with the wrong reason ('softer than a lump'), so the reason must be known. Key, context and fact unchanged.

dff0250687.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'It mixes in air, and the air dissolves the salt' was silly. It is replaced, as the judge proposed, by 'It helps the salt react with the water sooner' (dissolving taken for a reaction, M4), and the context now says dissolving is no reaction (F6). Stem, key and fact unchanged.

867ec165db.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'It drops to none, as the gas boils away' was silly at 30 degrees, and opening on the fish in a hot summer signalled harm. The silly choice is replaced, as the judge proposed, by 'It stays the same, as the air above it has not changed', and the stem now opens on the oxygen in the pond's water, with the fish left to the context. Judge (low): 'dissolved in its water' could be read as the fish's water; the stem now says 'the water of a pond'. Same key and fact (F24-F26).

1b652460f3.why: Judge (high, tell): the stem stated the mechanism (gas forced in under pressure, the bottle capped tight) and 'chilled' ruled out boiling. As the judge proposed, the stem is now just the sealed bottle and the bubbles on opening, and the bottling plant moves to the context. The bottle stands on a shelf, not at a table, to keep it out of the kitchen lane. Same key idea and fact (F27, F28).

dropped.question: A chemist makes a deep purple solution of potassium permanganate. She measures 10 millilitres of it into a flask and adds 90 millilitres of water, and the liquid turns a much paler purple. How much permanganate does the flask hold now, compared with the 10 millilitres she poured in?
dropped.why: failed the re-check: The old error is fixed: 'a much paler purple' is right for one tenfold step, since deep purple is above about 1e-2 M and pale pink below about 1e-4 M. But the new lure, 'Less, as the water has broken some of it down', is not cleanly wrong, and the context answers it with a false sentence. Grokipedia: 'In neutral aqueous solutions, potassium permanganate undergoes slow disproportionation' to manganese dioxide, so 'Water does not break the permanganate down' teaches an untruth. The lure fails only because the breakdown is too slow to matter in the minutes since she poured. Fix: use a lure that is false on any timescale, and drop or qualify the water sentence ('in so short a time, the water breaks none of it down').
